blocks.html:
This is the first thing a core developer does on the legacy (Docker Compose) stack: get pvarki/docker-rasenmaeher-integration running locally with the core rmapi built from source, so you can edit it and see changes live. Everything here comes from the compose repo's README.rst "Running in local development mode" section.

Prerequisites

  • Docker with Compose v2.
  • The repo cloned with submodules (the core lives in the api/ submodule):
git clone --recurse-submodules -j8 git@github.com:pvarki/docker-rasenmaeher-integration.git

If you forgot --recurse-submodules, run git submodule update --init --recursive.

Windows: use WSL and fix line endings

From the README.rst "Windows notes":

  • Do not use git-bash — it causes the weirdest issues with Docker containers.
  • Use WSL (setup instructions live in pvarki/markdown-pvarki-best_practises).
  • Make sure your git client / IDE does not rewrite line endings:

git config --global core.eol lf
git config --global core.autocrlf false

1. Start the local registry

Due to BuildKit cache bugs, the dev compositions push/pull through a local registry on port 5050. Start it once:
docker run -d -p 5050:5000 --restart always --name registry registry:3

2. Pick a composition: rmlocal vs rmdev

The repo provides two compose aliases. Define whichever you need:

alias rmlocal="PVARKI_DOCKER_REPO=localhost:5050/ docker compose -p rmlocal -f docker-compose-local.yml"
alias rmdev="PVARKI_DOCKER_REPO=localhost:5050/ docker compose -p rmdev -f docker-compose-local.yml -f docker-compose-dev.yml"

• **rmlocal** corresponds best to a real running environment — assets are minified and baked in. Start here, and always verify your changes work in rmlocal before trusting rmdev.
  • **rmdev** layers docker-compose-dev.yml on top and runs the core in development mode. This is the convenient inner-loop environment but introduces extra variability.

Note: If you only want to test the stack and not build your own changes, drop the PVARKI_DOCKER_REPO=localhost:5050/ prefix from the alias to use pre-built images.

3. Build and bring it up

Build the special init/cert images (pushing them to the local registry), then build the rest, then start:

rmdev build takinit miniwerk rmnginx --pull --push
rmdev build --pull
rmdev up

(Substitute rmlocal for rmdev if running the baked-in composition.) OpenLDAP and keycloak-init sometimes fail on first start — just run up again.

4. How rmdev hot-reloads the core

In rmdev, the rmapi service is built from the ./api submodule with the source bind-mounted into the container (./api:/app) and launched under uvicorn reload:

As the README.rst puts it: the dev version runs rasenmaeher-api in uvicorn reload mode, so any edits you make under /api are soon reflected in the running instance. That is the core inner loop — see Iterate on the core API (Docker Compose).

Note: If the rasenmaeher-ui dev server complains, delete uiv2/node_modules on the host first — the Docker Node.js distribution likely is not compatible with whatever is installed on the host.

6. Get first-admin access

Generate the first admin invite code in local mode:
rmlocal exec rmapi -it /bin/bash -c "source /.venv/bin/activate && rasenmaeher_api addcode"

Then log in through the UI, enter the code, and choose your admin callsign (the operator flow is described in the Operate book).

Shipping a core change

The core you are editing lives in the api/ submodule (pvarki/python-rasenmaeher-api), which is its own repo. The aggregate compose repo only records which commit of that submodule it points at. So a core change ships in two steps:

  1. In the submodule (cd api/): branch, commit, push, and open a PR to pvarki/python-rasenmaeher-api. Get it merged.
  2. In the compose repo: open a PR that updates the submodule pointer to the merged commit (check out the merged commit/tag inside api/, then git add api at the repo root, commit, and PR).

The full submodule-PR + compose-edit workflow — including what to do for a brand-new product integration — is documented in Build an Integration > Register your integration (Docker Compose); follow it there rather than reinventing it.

Keeping environments sane

These two rules from the README.rst prevent most local pain:

  • Only keep one of **rmlocal** / **rmdev** up at a time. Running both causes network issues. Run down for one before starting the other.
  • Run **down -v** to reset persistent volumes when switching environments or when you hit weird state. Note that down -v deletes certificates and users — you will have to re-add everything.
